extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science, civic educators, policymakers and informed citizens interested in public opinion and democratic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies Lippmann’s criteria for when and how the mass public should judge controversies, accept spokesmen, and support reforms; includes procedural tests for rules and principles of public opinion useful for civic education and policy evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization of spokesmen
rubrics_metrics.description: The public must look to see whether the spokesman is authorized; it must tell whether the representative is able to give assent by committing his constituency to a course of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden of proof is thrown on those who deny that an apparent leader (vested with external signs of office) is the real leader. Between nations, unless there is open rebellion or an impending election, public opinion cannot go behind official returns; settlements must be made with the government in office. Within associations (e.g., unions), an employer should accept leaders as authorized unless the union itself impeaches them; if leaders are challenged internally, the public must use rough external criteria to judge whether spokesmen can commit their constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of assent
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of assent by large bodies of men is simply that their spokesmen have agreed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance of a course of action by the recognized spokesmen is the public’s standard for assuming collective commitment. This general principle is modified when there is evident opposition or internal challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Open criticism of a rule is likely to be accompanied by or followed by evasion; widespread criticism is a surface symptom that the rule is unstable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a rule is frequently broken rather than occasionally, it is defective — it 'does not define the conduct which normally may be expected.' The public can detect the presence of a defect by the tests of assent and conformity, though it cannot usually diagnose the precise cause of the defect (e.g., bad adjustment, obscurity, lack of interpreting machinery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing the importance of opposition (rough external criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: In estimating a challenge to leadership the public’s concern is how far the Opposition can, by numbers, strategic importance, or determination, impair the value of an assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public should use only rough, external indicators (numbers, strategic position, evidence of rebellion). Only opposition that threatens nonconformity matters; criticism that does not challenge credentials is an internal affair. If spokesmen are elected, their assent is reliable until a new election; if non-elective and a rebellious opposition is evident, their assent is tentative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Note which party is least willing to submit its whole claim to inquiry and to abide by the result; willingness to accept inquiry is a clue to sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where facts are obscure and precedents lacking, the public should judge which claimant will submit to impartial inquiry or propose a tribunal. Acceptance of inquiry creates an atmosphere of reason, offers a prospect of settlement or delay of summary action, and tends to isolate the most arbitrary disputants. This principle is invoked for nonjusticiable international questions and similar complex disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule must provide for its own clarification/interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule should be so clear that a violation is apparent, and must contain a settled procedure by which it can be interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no general rule covers all cases, a good rule must include means for its own clarification so breaches are undeniably overt and experience can reveal defects. Example: a treaty that requires evacuation when 'conditions are fulfilled' is defective unless it defines those conditions or provides interpretation procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for amendment and public procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule must be organized so that it can be amended (so deadlock may be dissolved) and should provide that, subject to a formal procedure, controversy over revision shall be public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendment must be possible even when assent is not forthcoming; public procedure for revision helps break obstruction. However, amendment should not be continual or unforeseen — stability requires that amendment be allowed only after due notice appropriate to the affected parties (longer notice for those with long commitments, shorter for others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three procedural tests for judging a new rule (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a new rule the public should ask: Does it provide for its own clarification? For its own amendment by consent? For due notice that amendment will be proposed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tests are designed to assess the prospects of a settlement by its procedure rather than by its substantive merits. A reform satisfying these tests is normally entitled to public support. (Note: Lippmann emphasizes amendment must be possible but not capricious; 'by consent' signals legitimate, public procedures for revision.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive action is not for the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The public acts only by aligning itself as the partisan of someone in a position to act executively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public is not the direct executor of policy; it should judge and align with actors who have executive capacity. This limits the proper role of mass public action to choosing between actors rather than performing executive functions itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic merits and technical handling are not for the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The intrinsic merits of a question, its anticipation, analysis and solution, and the specific technical intimate criteria required are not for the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public judgment rests on small samples of facts and generalized criteria; detailed, technical, or intimate aspects are the province of insiders (experts, officials). Civic education should therefore teach the public usable procedural canons rather than attempt to turn citizens into expert executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public’s criteria should be generalized and procedural
rubrics_metrics.description: The public’s criteria are generalized for many problems; they turn essentially on procedure and the overt, external forms of behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the public cannot judge technical substance, it should focus on external indicators (procedural regularity, openness, adherence to settled rules) to distinguish reasonable from arbitrary behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable behavior = following a settled course
rubrics_metrics.description: For social action, reasonable behavior is conduct which follows a settled course whether in making a rule, in enforcing it or in amending it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operational definition lets the public sample external behavior to judge actors. It assigns political scientists the task of devising sampling methods and civic education the role of training the public in those methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of usable tests determines whether to intervene
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a usable test is itself the test of whether the public ought to intervene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no applicable tests exist (i.e., the public cannot reduce the dispute to the kinds of procedural or external samples it can judge), the wisest course is neutrality or abstention rather than blind partisanship; intervention without usable tests is likely to produce muddle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic: prefer Outs when Ins are compromised
rubrics_metrics.description: Normally the public must turn to the Outs as against the Ins when the Ins become committed to particular interests and lose neutral freedom of decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public’s broad judgment in elections is cumulative: support Ins when problems are being solved, support Outs when problems are being aggravated. The Outs’ virtue lies in not being committed to the overweighted particular interests of the Ins; this is a coarse, practical heuristic rather than a substantive test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit public intervention to its capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper limits of intervention by the public are determined by its capacity to make judgments; where it cannot use the tests, it should refrain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many problems cannot be advanced by the public’s 'obtuse partisanship.' When issues are too confused or subtle for the public’s tests to apply, abstention ('keep an open mind and wait to see') is preferable to meddling.
